deep.reconstruction:
Context (previous page). This is the projection of a planetary orbit onto the ecliptic. Notation: e = sin φ; a is the semi-major axis; E is the eccentric anomaly; i is the inclination; Ω is the node; g = ϖ − Ω is the argument of perihelion; λ is the heliocentric longitude; ρ is the curtate distance.

In the orbital plane, with the x-axis toward perihelion, the planet is at (a(cosE − e), a cosφ sinE). Rotating by g about the node line and multiplying the out-of-node component by cos i gives
  ρ (cos(λ−Ω), sin(λ−Ω))ᵀ = M (cosE − e, sinE)ᵀ,
  M = a [[cos g, −cosφ sin g], [cos i sin g, cosφ cos i cos g]].
Gauss defines α, 𝔟, γ, ε by four equations:
  (α−𝔟)cos(γ−ε) = a(1−cosφ cos i)cos g
  (α−𝔟)sin(γ−ε) = a(cos i−cosφ)sin g
  (α+𝔟)cos(γ+ε) = a(1+cosφ cos i)cos g
  (α+𝔟)sin(γ+ε) = a(cos i+cosφ)sin g

This page.
(1) Claim: with these quantities,
  α cos(E+ε) − α e cos ε = ρ cos(λ−γ−Ω),
  𝔟 sin(E+ε) − 𝔟 e sin ε = ρ sin(λ−γ−Ω).
In matrix form this says M = R(γ)·diag(α,𝔟)·R(ε), where R is a rotation. That is a 2×2 singular value decomposition.
Proof (mine): write diag(α,𝔟) = ½(α+𝔟)I + ½(α−𝔟)J with J = diag(1,−1). Then R(γ)R(ε) = R(γ+ε) and R(γ)JR(ε) = [[cos(γ−ε), sin(γ−ε)], [sin(γ−ε), −cos(γ−ε)]]. Hence
  M11+M22 = (α+𝔟)cos(γ+ε),
  M21−M12 = (α+𝔟)sin(γ+ε),
  M11−M22 = (α−𝔟)cos(γ−ε),
  M21+M12 = (α−𝔟)sin(γ−ε).
These are exactly the four defining equations.
Interpretation, as Gauss states it: the projected orbit is an ellipse with semi-axes α, 𝔟. Its centre lies at (−αe cos ε, −𝔟e sin ε) in the frame whose abscissa is the axis 2α. That axis makes angle γ+Ω with the equinoctial line. The eccentric-type anomaly in the projected ellipse is E+ε, a constant shift of E.

(2) Auxiliary angles: tan k = cos i (Gauss first wrote cos k, then corrected it to cos i), tan l = cos φ, c = a/(cos k cos l). Then
  a(1−cosφ cos i) = c cos(k+l)
  a(cos i−cosφ) = c sin(k−l)
  a(1+cosφ cos i) = c cos(k−l)
  a(cos i+cosφ) = c sin(k+l)
These follow from 1 ∓ tan k tan l = cos(k±l)/(cos k cos l) and tan k ∓ tan l = sin(k∓l)/(cos k cos l).

(3) Example: Juno, elements for 1810.
Inputs: φ = 14°45′35″, log a = 0.42648, i = 13°4′12″, Ω = 171°7′48″, ϖ = 53°10′52″, so g = ϖ−Ω = 242°3′4″. Also recorded: epoch mean longitude 95°33′50″; daily motion 813.5165″ tropical and 813.379″ sidereal (the difference ≈ precession per day).
Basic logs: log cosφ = 9.9854277; log cos i = 9.9886011; log e = log sinφ = 9.4061415.
Auxiliary angles: l = 44°2′20.14″, k = 44°14′53.40″.
Then log cos k + log cos l = 9.7117586, so log c = 0.42648 − 9.71176 = 0.71472.
Sums and differences: k+l = 88°17′13.54″ and k−l = 0°12′33.26″, giving
  log cos(k+l) = 8.47555, log sin(k+l) = 9.99981,
  log cos(k−l) = 0.00000, log sin(k−l) = 7.56252.
Products with c: c·cos(k+l) → 9.19027; c·cos(k−l) → 0.71472; c·sin(k−l) → 8.27724; c·sin(k+l) → 0.71453.
With log cos g = 9.67088n and log sin g = 9.94614n:
  (α+𝔟)cos(γ+ε) → 0.38560n
  (α+𝔟)sin(γ+ε) → 0.66067n
  so γ+ε = 242°2′26″, log sin(γ+ε) = 9.94610, log(α+𝔟) = 0.71457.
  (α−𝔟)cos(γ−ε) → 8.86115n
  (α−𝔟)sin(γ−ε) → 8.22338n
  so γ−ε = 192°58′2″, log cos(γ−ε) = 9.98878, log(α−𝔟) = 8.87237.
Hence ε = 24°32′12″, γ = 217°30′14″, and γ+Ω = 388°38′2″ ≡ 28°38′2″.
Axes: log 2α = 0.72077 and log 2𝔟 = 0.70828, so log α = 0.41974 and log 𝔟 = 0.40725. The value of e is unchanged (9.40614).
Centre coordinates ('Coord. C.'):
  αe → 9.82588; with log cos ε 9.95890 this gives −0.60923.
  𝔟e → 9.81339; with log sin ε 9.61834 this gives −0.27022.
A boxed first attempt for γ−ε, γ, ε, γ+Ω is struck out; it apparently had a quadrant or sign slip, giving γ = 232°16′34″. It was replaced by the correct values.
errors: No substantive errors. The formulas on this page and the previous one are correct; I checked them via the 2×2 decomposition M = R(γ) diag(α,𝔟) R(ε).
The definition line first read 'cos k = tang k'; Gauss corrected it to 'cos i = tang k'.
A first numerical attempt is struck out: 8.86115 not marked negative, 222°30′42″, γ = 232°16′34″, γ+Ω ≈ 43°24′. It reflects a quadrant/sign slip and is correctly superseded.
Numerical values check to the last place given, within ordinary 5–7 place log rounding. l computes to about 44°2′20.2″ against Gauss's 20.14″, which is negligible.

results.what: Orthogonal projection of a Keplerian ellipse onto the ecliptic. The projection is an ellipse with semi-axes α, 𝔟, axis orientation γ+Ω, centre (−αe cos ε, −𝔟e sin ε). The anomaly in it is E+ε, a constant shift.
results.modern_name: Affine image of an ellipse; principal axes of a projected orbit

results.what: Determination of α, 𝔟, γ, ε from the projection matrix via sums and differences of its entries: (α±𝔟)cos(γ±ε), (α±𝔟)sin(γ±ε). This is a closed-form factorisation M = R(γ) diag(α,𝔟) R(ε).
results.modern_name: 2×2 singular value decomposition (closed form via the rotation/reflection split)
results.usually_credited_to: General SVD: Beltrami 1873, Jordan 1874. The 2×2 axes-of-an-ellipse problem is classical (e.g., Rytz 1845 construction).

results.what: Auxiliary angles tan k = cos i, tan l = cos φ to make the four coefficients loggable products.
Numerical worked example for Juno (1810 elements): γ+Ω = 28°38′2″, log α = 0.41974, log 𝔟 = 0.40725, centre (−0.60923, −0.27022).

deep.surprise_reason: Elegant, correct closed-form 2×2 rotation–scaling–rotation factorisation (effectively a 2×2 SVD) applied to the projected orbit. However, the axes of an affinely mapped ellipse were a classical problem, and the technique is typical of Gauss's computational astronomy. It is a nice unpublished detail but not a result usually credited to someone later in a way that matters.

transcription_corrections: In the definitions, Gauss first wrote 'cos k' and corrected it to 'cos i' (= tang k); the transcription's markup is right in substance.
In the struck-out box, 'ε = 19.45.52' is probably '9.45.52', consistent with (242°2′26″ − 222°30′42″)/2.

The values under cos g (9.19027, 0.71472) are log c·cos(k+l) and log c·cos(k−l). Those under sin g (8.27724, 0.71453) are log c·sin(k−l) and log c·sin(k+l). They are intermediate products, not new quantities.
9.94610 is log sin(γ+ε) and 9.98878 is log cos(γ−ε).
